source.title: On the Design of Qwen3.8-Next Architecture: Evaluation, Efficiency, and Training Stability
source.authors: Zi-Han Qiu; Ze-Kun Wang; Xiao Li; Yan-Peng Li; Yang Xu; Yi-Xuan Wang; Hua-Qing Zhang; Rui Men; Bowei Mao; Chengruidong Zhang; Fan Zhou; Hao Luo; Haoran Huang; Hao-Ran Lian; Hao-Yan Huang; Hongqing Chen; Jian-Wei Zhang; Jing Xu; Junjie Wang; Langshi Chen; Liang-Yu Wang; Lintong Jiang; Man Yuan; Minmin Sun; Peng Jin; Si-Qi Zhang; Si-Yu Wang; Xing-Zhang Ren; Yakai Wang; Yi Zhang; Yiman Dong; Yi-Zhong Cao; Yu-Bo Ma; Yun-Fei Mao; Bo Zheng; Dayiheng Liu

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses a refitted scaling law to choose learning rates and batch sizes, then tests those hyperparameter predictions. It does not test the claimed power laws for held-out loss versus model parameters, tokens, or compute, or the claimed compute-optimal parameter/token split.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for learning-rate and batch-size scaling, which are related but not versions of the requested loss-scaling or compute-optimal allocation claims. The rows below record these distinct hyperparameter-scaling findings as versions ["none"]. Citations to scaling-law findings from other work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The paper is mainly an architecture report that refits a hyperparameter scaling law, which bears on no version. However, its own ablations bear on V6: loss and downstream accuracy diverge. In Tab. 9, n-gram vocabulary scaling (more parameters) lowers loss monotonically, 1.585→1.526, while several benchmarks saturate or fall. In Tab. 5, a 0.002 loss change comes with a 1.98-point benchmark gain. Elsewhere, large loss gaps do track benchmarks (Tab. 10). This is a specific result that V6 holds only partially.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also stress that loss and downstream accuracy do not always move together. For example, enlarging the n-gram vocabulary lowers loss while accuracy saturates, so they check benchmarks alongside loss. They also conclude that architecture, efficiency and optimization form one coupled design problem.
record.recipe_differences: The paper does not reproduce the original loss-versus-parameters/tokens/compute method or test compute-optimal model/data allocation. It refits a hyperparameter scaling law for a changed architecture and optimizer, focusing on learning rate and batch size.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors state that optimal learning rate and batch size depend on architecture and optimizer. They also compare constant and ramped batch schedules, and vary learning rate and batch size around the predicted setting.

fits_no_version.finding: A learning-rate and batch-size scaling law refitted for a new architecture and Muon optimizer predicts near-optimal settings at 4T tokens (10.8B-A0.89B) and at 156B-A7B. Batch-size warmup gives no gain.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hyperparameter (LR/batch) scaling laws fitted at small scale extrapolate to near-optimal settings at larger scale and token budgets.

record.problems: The hyperparameter predictions are tested in selected regimes rather than as a comprehensive test of loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute. The paper notes that single-run benchmark rankings and narrow margins may be within evaluation noise.
record.rows_left_out: No results on downstream benchmarks, architecture comparisons, or training stability are included because they do not test the claim versions. The paper does not report tested power-law exponents, compute-optimal parameter/token allocations, or loss extrapolations of the kind specified in the claim.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of loss against parameters, tokens or compute. Tab. 9 shows only monotonic loss decrease over 5 n-gram vocabulary sizes.
No loss extrapolation. The extrapolation tested is for learning-rate and batch-size predictions, not loss.
No depth/width sweep at fixed parameter count. The residual and attention ablations change architecture type, not shape.
No comparison of loss-law exponents or of the compute-optimal split across fitting choices.
Downstream performance as a function of model size or compute is not tested. Only how well downstream accuracy tracks loss is examined.

missing.what: N-gram vocabulary scaling: loss versus downstream benchmarks. Loss falls monotonically while benchmarks saturate or decline.
Fixed-budget n-gram allocation: loss optimum at 10× vocabulary not matched by uncheatable PPL or benchmarks.
Residual ablation: mHC static to dynamic gives 0.002 loss but a 1.98-point average benchmark gain, against 0.021 loss and 1.58 points from baseline to static.
Hyperparameter runs: loss gap of 7.8e-3 aligns with a benchmark average of 60.55 vs 56.41. Near-optimum settings within 7e-4 loss have similar averages.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T4/uses_without_test is reasonable for the hyperparameter content. However, the loss–downstream divergence results are the study's own and bear on V6, so the relation is upgraded to tests/T5. No rows capture these results; the V6 verdicts rest on the text, and rows should be added per 'missing'. Existing rows r1–r6 correctly carry versions ['none'].

versions.untested_parts: Not tested: power-law held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Not tested: extrapolating loss power laws fitted on small runs to much larger runs.
Not tested: compute-optimal parameter and token allocation or their growth with compute.
Not tested: loss sensitivity to depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Not tested: power-law loss scaling in other modalities or training regimes.
The paper reports downstream benchmark scores, but does not test whether downstream performance improves predictably with model scale or pretraining loss.

The paper says architecture and optimizer changes shift optimal learning rate and batch size, but does not test dependence of loss-scaling exponents or the compute-optimal parameter/token split on setup or fitting choices.

relationships.condition: N-gram embedding vocabulary scaling (extra parameters) and small-loss-gap architecture changes on MoE models
relationships.reason: Text-based (no rows). Tab. 9: loss falls 1.585→1.526 from 20× to 200× vocabulary, while MATH 37.38→35.34 and GSM8K 65.09→62.96 fall. Tab. 8: the loss optimum is not the accuracy optimum. Tab. 5: 0.002 loss change but a 1.98-point gain.
relationships.display_finding: Increasing vocabulary from 20× to 200× lowered loss from 1.585 to 1.526 but reduced MATH from 37.38 to 35.34 and GSM8K from 65.09 to 62.96; other architecture comparisons separated loss and accuracy optima and paired a 0.002 loss change with a 1.98-point gain.

relationships.condition: Large loss gaps from hyperparameter recipe change at 156B-A7B, 419B tokens
relationships.reason: Text-based (no rows). The previous recipe has 7.8e-3 higher loss and a 56.41 vs 60.55 benchmark average (Tab. 10). Lower loss tracks better downstream here.
relationships.display_finding: The previous recipe had 0.0078 higher loss and a benchmark average of 56.41, compared with 60.55 for the revised recipe.
